The eggs of the Greater short-toed lark (Calandrella brachydactyla) are subelliptical and measure between 17.4 and 22.8 mm in length with a width ranging from 12.9 to 16 mm, yielding a calculated initial wet weight of 1.36 grams [Ww0 = 1.36 grams]. This modest egg mass is typical for an open-country passerine that must balance energy investment against the risks of ground-level predation. When incubated at a temperature of 32 °C [T = 32 °C], hatching occurs after approximately 12 days [ab = approximately 12 days], which aligns closely with the 11 to 13 day range reported from field studies in Mediterranean steppe habitats. The nestlings emerge as altricial chicks and are entirely dependent on parental provisioning for both warmth and food during their initial days. This relatively short incubation period likely reflects the species’ adaptation to hot, arid environments where extended exposure on the nest would increase vulnerability to solar radiation and opportunistic predators.

Under the thermal conditions associated with active metabolism in adults (40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]), the post-hatching developmental schedule follows a distinct trajectory. Fledging, defined as the achievement of sustained flight and nest departure, occurs at 13.5 days after hatching [tx = 13.5 days after hatching], a value consistent with the 12 to 15 day range documented across European breeding populations at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This rapid transition from nestling to fledgling status is characteristic of larks that inhabit open landscapes, where the need to escape terrestrial threats selects for early flight capability. The downy chicks develop pin feathers quickly and are capable of short flights by the end of the second week, although they continue to be fed by the parents for several days after leaving the nest. Such a developmental pace contrasts with that of forest-dwelling passerines, which often experience longer nestling periods under the relative safety of dense canopy cover.

Sexual maturation in this species proceeds on a similarly accelerated schedule when ambient temperatures approximate 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. The time since birth at puberty for female Greater short-toed larks is 40.5 days [tp = 40.5 days], indicating that individuals can become reproductively active within their first summer if conditions are favorable. at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]This early onset of gonadal activity is remarkable for a small-bodied alaudid and likely represents an adaptive response to short breeding windows in seasonally arid environments. Field observations suggest that young females rarely breed in their first year, despite reaching physiological maturity, because competition for territories and the energetic demands of egg production constrain actual reproduction. Nonetheless, the potential for rapid maturation underscores a life-history strategy that prioritizes early readiness over extended somatic growth, consistent with patterns observed in other arid-zone passerines such as the Lesser short-toed lark.

The first successful breeding attempt typically occurs at 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching] when maintained at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], which corresponds to the onset of the second calendar year. Females produce a single clutch annually [F_R_i = single clutch annually], with each clutch containing 4 eggs [N_R_i = each clutch containing 4 eggs]. This moderate reproductive investment is typical of many temperate-zone alaudids and likely reflects the trade-off between current fecundity and adult survival in a variable environment. The timing of this first brood is synchronized with spring insect emergence, ensuring maximal food availability for the rapidly growing nestlings. Comparative data from closely related congeners suggest that the Greater short-toed lark occupies an intermediate position on the slow-fast life-history continuum: faster than the long-lived Horned Lark but slower than the highly prolific Sky Lark. The maximum recorded longevity for this species reaches approximately 8.7 years [am = approximately 8.7 years] at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], a lifespan that allows multiple reproductive episodes and contributes to population stability despite high nest predation rates.

Basal metabolic measurements for the Greater short-toed lark reveal a maximum oxygen consumption of approximately 73.4 milliliters per hour [JOi = approximately 73.4 milliliters per hour] when assessed at the active metabolic temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This value, derived from respirometry trials on captive individuals, corresponds to a mass-specific metabolic rate that is modest relative to other passerines of comparable body mass. The ultimate wet weight for adult females has been recorded at 21.1 grams [Wwi = 21.1 grams], placing the species among the smaller representatives of the genus Calandrella. This relatively low body mass, combined with a moderate metabolic rate, likely facilitates the high field metabolic demands imposed by foraging in open, sun-exposed habitats where thermoregulatory costs are substantial. The interplay between body size, metabolic expenditure, and thermal environment provides a framework for understanding the species’ biogeographic distribution across the Palearctic region. Populations at the northern edge of the range may face elevated energetic challenges compared with their Mediterranean and North African conspecifics.
